common_name: Clown Blue Torenia (Compact Blue Wishbone Flower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or set transplants out once frost danger has passed, into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Clown Blue's two-tone light and deep blue snapdragon-like markings read best in beds and color bowls viewed up close.

directions: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist, well-drained, fertile soil, where Clown Blue's compact, early, well-branched habit fills a bed or container faster than many other torenia selections. The tubular flowers show two shades of blue, a lighter upper lip over a deeper blue lower lip, giving more depth of color than solid-blue bedding annuals. It blooms continuously from late spring through frost without deadheading and tolerates summer heat and humidity better than most other shade annuals, though direct afternoon sun will bleach the color and slow flowering. Keep soil evenly damp, since torenia's shallow roots dry out and stall bloom production quickly once stressed.

common_name: White Bells Browallia (Classic White Bush Violet)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, or set transplants out once frost danger has passed, into moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; White Bells pairs well with the companion Blue Bells selection already grown in this dataset for a two-tone hanging basket.

directions: Grow in partial to full shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, where White Bells produces an abundance of pure white, bell-shaped flowers over mounded, slightly trailing foliage. Its clean white coloring brightens dim corners and container plantings more effectively than the violet-blue Browallia selections already represented in this dataset, and it mixes well with darker shade-loving companions. The plant flowers continuously from early summer through frost and needs no deadheading, but performance drops quickly if the shallow root zone is allowed to dry out in summer heat. Pinch young plants once to encourage bushier growth and a fuller bloom display in beds, baskets, or window boxes.

common_name: Techno Heat Dark Blue Lobelia (Heat-Tolerant Trailing Deep Blue Lobelia)

planting.note: Set out transplants from early spring through the point when nights stay reliably warm, into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Techno Heat Dark Blue holds its intense color and keeps blooming through summer heat that stalls older edging lobelia strains.

directions: Plant in partial shade, especially where afternoon sun is filtered, in evenly moist, fertile, well-drained soil, since the Techno Heat series was bred specifically to keep flowering through summer conditions that cause most Lobelia erinus selections to stall and decline. Techno Heat Dark Blue carries saturated deep blue flowers over a mounding, semi-trailing habit suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and the front of shaded borders. Unlike the earlier-blooming Techno Heat White already grown in this dataset, the Dark Blue selection gives the richest, most concentrated color of the series for contrast plantings. Keep soil consistently moist, since lobelia's fine, shallow roots dry out and stop flowering quickly in hot weather.

common_name: Laguna Dark Blue Lobelia (Vegetative Trailing Deep Blue Lobelia)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated transplants from early spring through the point nights stay reliably warm, into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Laguna Dark Blue trails further than seed-grown lobelia strains, making it well suited to hanging baskets and tall containers.

directions: Grow in partial shade with some protection from hot afternoon sun, in consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil, since the Laguna series is a Proven Winners vegetative line bred for stronger heat tolerance and longer trailing stems than seed-raised edging lobelia. Laguna Dark Blue bears true deep blue, self-cleaning flowers over trailing stems that can reach two feet, making it well suited to hanging baskets and window boxes rather than flat bedding use like the compact Riviera Sky Blue already grown in this dataset. It flowers from spring through frost without deadheading, but like all lobelia it needs steady soil moisture and will decline quickly if allowed to dry out repeatedly. Light trims after the first flush of bloom help keep the trailing stems full through the rest of the season.

common_name: Blue Moon Lobelia (Compact Violet-Blue Edging Lobelia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, or set out transplants once frost danger has passed, into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Blue Moon's compact mounding habit suits edging and small container plantings rather than the trailing baskets favored by Laguna and Techno Heat types.

directions: Plant in partial shade to lightly filtered sun, in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, where Blue Moon forms a low, leafy, branching mound covered in small deep violet-blue flowers from summer to frost. It is one of the older, longer-established Lobelia erinus selections and stays compact rather than trailing, making it a reliable choice for edging walkways and the front of shaded beds rather than hanging baskets. The plant tends to self-sow lightly where conditions suit it, so volunteer seedlings may appear the following year in beds left undisturbed. Keep the shallow root zone consistently moist through summer heat, since lobelia wilts and stops flowering quickly once the soil dries out.
